title: CEO Interview with Phillip Stanley-Marbell of Signaloid - Semiwiki
gist: Signaloid CEO Phillip Stanley-Marbell describes UxHw, a 'distribution-extended compute hardware' architecture that propagates probability-distribution metadata through ordinary floating-point programs to replace slow Monte Carlo-style simulation with single-pass computation, citing production deployments at Boeing, CERN and banks with 40x-1000x speedups, a May 2026 ASIC tape-out, and plans to bring the technology into AI data centers.

insights.claim: Signaloid's core technology, 'distribution-extended compute hardware' (UxHw), attaches probability-distribution metadata to floating-point values as a program runs, enabling algorithms to achieve 10-fold to 100-fold performance improvements, often with minimal code changes.
insights.speaker: Phillip Stanley-Marbell
insights.so_what: A general-purpose 10-100x speedup claim across simulation-heavy workloads (robotics, finance, chip design, pharma) positions UxHw as a potential efficiency layer investors should track alongside compute-hardware accelerators.
insights.quote: allows algorithms for these target applications to achieve 10-fold to 100-fold performance improvements, often with minimal changes.
insights.locator: Our core technology, which we call

insights.claim: UxHw's technical approach augments each floating-point operation in a program to also carry an in-machine representation of a continuous probability distribution, letting software that previously needed iterative sample-based methods like Monte Carlo simulation run in a single pass instead.
insights.speaker: Phillip Stanley-Marbell
insights.so_what: Replacing iterative Monte Carlo sampling with single-pass distribution arithmetic is the specific mechanism behind Signaloid's speedup claims, useful for technically evaluating whether the approach generalizes to a given workload.
insights.locator: The transformation we apply to programs

insights.claim: Signaloid quotes concrete production speedups from UxHw: 400x for risk analysis in critical infrastructure such as power plants, and 70x for bank-regulated risk modeling such as Solvency II, alongside 40x for circuit simulation using the ngspice simulator and 60x for event generators in high-energy physics simulations.
insights.speaker: Phillip Stanley-Marbell
insights.so_what: Order-of-magnitude speedups in regulator-mandated risk modeling (Solvency II) and critical-infrastructure risk analysis suggest a real cost/time reduction case for banks and utilities, a concrete enterprise-adoption driver to watch.
insights.quote: our enterprise platform provides 400x speedups for risk analysis in critical infrastructure such as power plants, 70x speedups for bank-regulated risk modeling (e.g., Solvency II)

insights.claim: In robotics and industrial-automation use cases, Signaloid's hardware module delivers up to 1000x speedup for sensor calibration margining and roughly 30x speedup for particle-filter state-estimation algorithms, such as those used in drones.
insights.speaker: Phillip Stanley-Marbell
insights.so_what: Extreme speedups in sensor calibration could materially cut development and compute cost for robotics and drone makers deploying probabilistic state-estimation algorithms.

insights.claim: Signaloid's enterprise UxHw platform is already deployed with Boeing, CERN, and major international banks for high-performance risk-analysis and simulation workloads.
insights.speaker: Phillip Stanley-Marbell
insights.so_what: Named enterprise customers in aerospace, physics research, and banking indicate the platform has moved past pilot stage into production use across multiple regulated, high-stakes industries.
insights.locator: we are working with companies like Boeing, CERN

insights.claim: Signaloid's hardware module for robotics and industrial automation is distributed through Bosch and Mouser, with active pilots underway at Infineon, ABB, and the German Aerospace Agency (DLR).
insights.speaker: Phillip Stanley-Marbell
insights.so_what: Distribution through a mainstream semiconductor distributor (Mouser) alongside pilots at established industrial-automation names signals a credible go-to-market channel beyond direct enterprise sales.
insights.locator: We have distribution partnerships with Bosch and Mouser

insights.claim: Signaloid taped out a new ASIC in May 2026 for its next generation of hardware modules, and holds more than 100 patent filings across the US, EU, Japan, China, and Taiwan.
insights.speaker: Phillip Stanley-Marbell
insights.so_what: A completed ASIC tape-out plus a sizeable multi-jurisdiction patent portfolio suggests real hardware execution and defensible IP, relevant for assessing the company's moat versus rival probabilistic-computing startups.
insights.quote: In May 2026, we taped out a new ASIC which will go into our future hardware modules.
insights.locator: In May 2026, we taped out a new ASIC

insights.claim: Signaloid's cloud compute engine runs on top of AWS and is ISO 27001 and SOC 2 Type II certified, positioning it for adoption by regulated enterprise customers such as banks.
insights.speaker: Phillip Stanley-Marbell
insights.so_what: Formal security certifications are often a prerequisite for enterprise/bank procurement, indicating Signaloid has cleared a compliance bar needed to sell into regulated finance customers at scale.
insights.locator: our Signaloid Cloud Compute Engine, which is built on top of AWS

insights.claim: Signaloid's recently taped-out ASIC is scheduled to go into a compute cluster deployment in the UK in the coming months, and the company plans to soon announce partnerships with major AI accelerator companies to bring UxHw technology into AI data centers.
insights.speaker: Phillip Stanley-Marbell
insights.so_what: A move into AI data centers via accelerator-company partnerships would be a significant expansion beyond Signaloid's current enterprise-risk and robotics niches, worth monitoring as a near-term catalyst.
insights.quote: we’ll soon be announcing partnerships with major AI accelerator companies to bring UxHw technology into AI data centers.

insights.claim: Signaloid frames its competitive landscape in two tiers: the classical-processor incumbents it aims to displace (Intel, AMD, Arm), and an emerging category the industry calls 'Probabilistic Computing,' which includes rival startups using either compact probability-distribution representations or physical material randomness.
insights.speaker: Phillip Stanley-Marbell
insights.so_what: Positions Signaloid within a nascent, still-forming competitive category rather than against an established incumbent product, which affects how quickly a moat can be defended versus rival startups.

insights.claim: Signaloid's stated differentiator versus other probabilistic-computing startups is having a proven, generally-available shipping product deployed on real applications, whereas it characterizes many competitors as having only research-paper or demo-video-stage technology.
insights.speaker: Phillip Stanley-Marbell
insights.so_what: If accurate, being first to a shipping, revenue-generating product in an emerging hardware category is a meaningful head start against research-stage competitors, though this claim comes from the company itself and should be independently verified.
insights.quote: We have a product that is proven to work in practice, whereas many competitors only have technology demonstrations in research papers (or YouTube videos)
insights.locator: Our key differentiators from other companies in this space
